Enough with this excessive detail;
looking ahead:
Ah! This blessed sun, the lamp for all the islands of the entire world, has risen to the greatest extent; I shall worship him.
Having prostrated, [I pray:
O Lord of universal form, you are the vessel of auspicious splendors;
therefore, bestow upon me most abundantly the preeminent fortune, and be gracious.
O Lord of the World, abandon whatever sin belongs to me as I bow before you; O Blessed One, bestow upon me every blessing for the sake of supreme auspiciousness.

Looking toward the tiring-room: Noble sir, the auspicious rites for the stage have been well performed, and people dwelling in various distant regions have gathered on the occasion of the festival of the holy Lord Kālapriyanātha.
I have been commanded by the assembly of learned men that we must be entertained by some unprecedented composition;
why then do the actors remain indifferent?
[Then] the assistant enters.

Sūtradhāra:
Noble sir, what are those merits that they cite therein? Ārya Vidagdha: [Listen.]
The venerable ones, the gods of the earth, and the actor are mixed together.

In that case, it is remembered:
what indeed is the actor's state?
Director: In the southern region of Vidarbha, there is a city named Padmanagara;
there lived certain teachers of the Taittirīya branch of the Kāśyapa lineage, who were purifiers of the assembly.

His wives were for the sake of offspring, and his life was for the sake of asceticism, belonging to that venerable one of well-remembered name, Bhaṭṭagopāla, who is the son of so-and-so.
The grandson of Nīlakaṇṭha, whose fame is purifying, the self-born son of Bhaṭṭa Śrīkaṇṭha,
named Bhavabhūti, was born of the lineage of Jātūkarṇī.

Our son, Kavi, out of natural affection for the descendants of Bharata, has thus offered us this work, which abounds in excellences of such a kind that it truly possesses this very power of expression.
As for those who spread contempt for us here,
they know nothing at all; this effort is not directed toward them.
"Someone of equal nature to me will surely arise;
for time is limitless and the earth is vast."

what is the use of mentioning the study of the Vedas, as well as the knowledge of the Upaniṣads, Sāṃkhya, and Yoga? For no quality whatsoever is derived from those in a drama.
Whatever maturity and loftiness there is in words, and whatever weightiness they possess by virtue of their meaning— if that exists, then that alone is the indicator of scholarship and wit.
Therefore, this very play entitled *Mālatīmādhava*, our own composition, a dear friend’s work entrusted to us by the venerable one named Bhavabhūti,
we intend to make known through performance before the illustrious Lord of Kālapriya.
"Let all those performers proceed with their musical performance in order to accomplish my desire."

Indeed, all the members of the group have been taught by Bhāva himself;
however, Bhāva alone has studied the first act of the Buddhist old nun Kāmandakī,
while I have studied that of her pupil, Avalokitā.

Kāmandakī:
Child Avalokitā!
Let the venerable lady Kāmandakī give her command.
"O lady with trembling eyes, may the desired marriage of those two auspicious ones, Mālatī and Mādhava— the offspring of Bhūrivasu and Devarāta—
come to pass," he said joyfully, having indicated it by the throbbing of his left eye.
As if revealing the inner excellence with the eye of one who possesses internal knowledge.
Even with her throbbing left hand,
Avalokita maintains courtesy.
Great indeed is this mental distraction of the Blessed One; it is a marvel,
a great marvel, that now [this] rag-robe...
The requisite of robes and the measure of almsfood.
Even for the sake of sustaining life, the minister Bhūrivasu directs the venerable lady to such great hardship as this. And there—
The self, by which the grasp of saṃsāra has been torn away, is being employed even by you.
Kāmandakī: Child, do not speak thus;
for you, sir, employ me in a matter that is within my power to perform.
This is the fruit of my affection, the very essence of my love; it is desired by me even at the cost of my life or my ascetic merits.
If a friend’s duty were to be fulfilled, then that would indeed have been done;
do you not realize, O friend, that we who dwell in various distant lands came together for the sole purpose of acquiring knowledge? And it was at that very time that our association occurred.

In the presence of Saudāminī, this vow was made by these two, Bhūrivasu and Devarāta: "We must certainly enter into a matrimonial alliance. Now, that [vow] being fulfilled by me while serving as the minister of the King of Vidarbha...
By Devarāta, who sent this Padmāvatī from the city of Kuṇḍina to Mādhava’s son for the purpose of hearing the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), a most excellent deed was performed.

A marvel! A marvel! Indeed, it is not so.

he must conceal his own intention.
Moreover,
there is indeed a common saying regarding attachment:

Behold how he,
while conducting himself in a manner outwardly perfect in every aspect and delightful,
conceals even the slightest grounds for another's suspicion.

remains indifferent while accomplishing his own ends and maintains silence.

Kāmandakī.

Well done, well done by the venerable Kāmandakī!
"Having reflected on that, arise, O Mādhava; let us go and see Mālatī herself once we have obtained news of her. Both rise.

"Mālatī is of an exceedingly noble nature; therefore, she is a skillful *nisṛṣṭārtha* messenger."
The plan must be carried out in every way so that she,
like the autumn moonlight, may delight him who is as lovely as a white water-lily;
may she be auspicious and well-born, and may that youth fulfill his purpose.
May the activity of the Creator, which is supremely excellent, skilled in fashioning mutually harmonious qualities, bear fruit and be pleasing to the mind.

then enters Kalahaṃsa, carrying painting materials.

The greatness of Malati’s heart, which has cast aside the pride, beauty, and bewilderment of the Fish-bannered God (Kamadeva).
I shall see my lord Mādhava;
having walked about,
I am exhausted, so until— here.

I shall see my lord Mādhava, the delight of Makaranda.

It has been told by Avalokitā that Mādhava has gone to the Madanodyāna; well then, I shall go there as well.

What indeed could this excessive sighing be? Could it be anything other than this? Or rather, the command of Kandarpa wanders through the world, and youth is subject to transformation.
Those various states of being, so charming and sweet, cast away even one's composure;
then enters Mādhava, as previously described.
Mādhava!
Having contemplated for a very long time that lady with a face as beautiful as the moon, my mind somehow, with great difficulty, turns away from her.
Having conquered shame, having warded off modesty, and having violently uprooted steadfastness,
discernment was suddenly destroyed.
It was a marvel that [the assembly] became motionless with wonder, with all other states of being extinguished, and languid with bliss as if from plunging into an ocean of nectar.
In his presence, my heart now remains throbbing with pain, as if touched by glowing coals.

Makaranda?

Mādhava:

Thus they both sit down.
Kalahaṃsaka, having seen him,
says: "How is it that this is Makaranda’s companion?"
Mādhava adorns this very Bālabakula garden; therefore—
I show him this Mālatī, who is tormented by the pangs of love.
A pleasing reflection of oneself for the eyes, or rather,
a source of rest and happiness for now.
Let Makaranda experience that very [fragrance],
first of all, which is astringent with the filaments of blossoming flowers.
"Let us sit beneath this kāñcanāra tree in the garden, which is scented with a cool fragrance.

Makaranda: Friend Mādhava, today indeed [the festival] has been inaugurated by all the women of the city.

I perceive you to be quite different from what you were when you returned from the festival procession to the garden of the god of love, so delightful with its great celebrations; could it be that even slightly...?
O Rati’s lover, you have entered the range of Bāṇa’s arrows;
that Mādhava stands with his face cast down in shame, and so does Makaranda.
Smiling, he said:
"Why do you stand with your charming lotus-face cast down? Behold, other living beings are shrouded in passion and ignorance."
He, the Mind-born, whose power is indeed well-known, is equal to the Creator of the universe and to the Supreme Lord.
Do not, out of shame, deny it in any way.
Friend Mādhava, why do you not speak? Listen: I went with Avalokitā.
His curiosity aroused, he wandered here and there through that temple of Kāmadeva,
and having looked about, he was refreshed by the sweet fragrance of wine arising from his exertion.

He stood in the vicinity of the basin of that young *bakula* tree, which was delightful with its charming ornaments in the form of rows of flower buds agitated by the swarms of bees gathering there, drawn by its fragrance; and which graced the courtyard ground.
And having gathered flowers that had fallen by chance without any interval between them,
I began to fashion a garland beautiful with its clever arrangement.

Immediately thereafter, like a moving victory banner for the conquest of the world by the god Makaraketana, she emerged from the inner apartments— a maiden whose radiant, clever, and charming attire revealed her youth.
O one of great majesty, some woman of noble nature and most generous retinue has come from that very place.

O friend, she is surely either the presiding deity of the treasure-house of loveliness, or the abode of the gathered essence of all beauty— she who is like the moon, nectar, and lotus stalks combined.
The moonlight and other such things became the cause, and Madana was the creator;
then she, together with her affectionate female companions who held dense clusters of flowers, [proceeded].

Requested by her female companions who were longing for the sport of gathering flowers, she came to that very spot beneath the *bakula* tree; and in some previous life of great merit, as it were, the god of love had been accumulating within her for many days.
I have observed a change caused by distress,
since her limbs are withered like crushed lotus stalks.
In some way, through the requests of her attendants,
she assumes the spotless splendor of the moon during her ritual acts.
Her cheek, pale as the fresh slice of an elephant’s tusk,
has since my first sight of her been like a magnet-stone to my eyes, generating an unsurpassed bliss as if it were a wick of nectar.
Like a probe drawing out metal ore, she completely extracted his inner heart;
what more need be said?
This mind, which is indifferent to its own cause and attached to that [stream of existence], leads to a continuous succession of torments and great calamities;
it generally brings about both the auspicious and the inauspicious for a living being.
Noble lady, destiny alone is all-consuming;
and as for Makaranda,
my friend Mādhava, and affection— they depend upon that very destiny as their cause.
Behold, this is contradictory:
some internal cause interweaves the constituent elements of things.
Indeed, joys do not depend upon external conditions;
for the white lotus blooms at the rising of the sun,
and the moonstone melts when the cold-rayed moon has emerged.
And so it was, and so it was,
said Mādhava.
Then, having made a play of her eyebrows there and looking at me as if with recognition, saying, "This is he," she— of her...

Of those eyes— sometimes steady, sometimes blossoming, with their creeper-like brows quivering, smooth and closed like buds, and possessing wide outer corners.

With eyes languid, rolling, charming, tender, motionless, and slow; with pupils wide open in wonder and smiling with their teeth more fully revealed.
My heart, having no refuge, has been stolen, cast away, drunk up, and uprooted by the side-glances of that long-lashed-eyed woman.

The side-glance of that long-lashed-eyed woman— resembling a lotus with its stalk turned back, and as if smeared with both nectar and poison—
is as if deeply embedded in my heart.
From that point onward,
it transcends all determination and is beyond the scope of every word.

Furthermore, that certain internal transformation which has not entered the path of experience in this birth— due to the destruction of discrimination and the dense thicket of great delusion it has accumulated— both numbs and causes torment.

"Friend, listen: then, at the very moment of her mounting the female elephant,

whose true form must be beheld, is the very cause of your transformation— therefore, it is right here.

Here I am, Saudāminī; having flown up from the venerable Śrīparvata, I have come to Padmāvatī.

Mālatī has taken refuge there with her circle of friends at the dwelling of Mādhava, who, unable to endure the sight of familiar places while separated from his beloved, has abandoned his residence and now dwells in the region of the great valley and mountain forest.
"Now, O sir, I am approaching your presence; I have flown up in such a way that this entire range of mountains, cities, villages, rivers,
and forests is visible to my eye."
Having looked around, he is subsequently surrounded;
"Excellent! Excellent! [he says].
Padmāvatī bears the guise of a surrounding circle of rivers— the Vimalā, the Vāri, the Viśālā, the Sindhu, and the Pārā.
And the sky, as if split open and released by the collision with lofty palaces, celestial temples, gate-towers, and attics; and—
This is that very Lavanā, shining with rows of graceful waves,
which at the onset of the clouds brings joy to the people, while her cattle carry burdens of beloved, fresh ulapa-grass and are pregnant.
Beholding from another direction, the circles of forests near the banks of the river being frequented shine forth.
This is that very bank of the blessed river Sindhu where the subterranean realm was rent asunder;
it is from here that this tumultuous sound issues forth, as fierce as the thundering of fresh clouds heavy with water.
Expanding within the groves of the surrounding mountains,
it attains the likeness of the roar from the throat of Ganesha.
And these mountain forest regions— dense with trees such as sandalwood, aśvakarṇa, kesara, and pāṭala, and fragrant with ripe wood-apples—
surely call to mind the valleys of the young kadamba and jambū groves.
And these mountains of the Southern Forest,
whose broad and lush slopes resound with the Godāvarī as it issues from deep,
dark, and heavy groves; and this river Madhumatī.
Having bowed down to the Lord, the husband of Bhavānī, who purifies through his confluence, whose foundation is not of human origin, and who is known as Suvarṇabindu;
Victory to you, O God, creator of the world! Victory to you, Blessed One, bestower of all boons,
treasure-house of the Vedas!
Victory to you, O beautiful one with the moon as your crest-jewel! Victory to you, O destroyer of Madana! Victory to you, O primordial teacher!
(Having thus enacted his departure:)
This mountain possesses lofty peaks dark as a fresh cloud;
its peacocks cry out with passion,
and its trees are lush in stature, their nests variegated by birds.
Moreover, Mount Bṛhadaśma delights the eyes.
Here, within the hollows of the caves,
the deep, resonant growls of young bears are echoed;
and the cold, pungent, and astringent resin of the sallakī trees solidifies.
The scent of the exudation from the crushed and scattered joints of elephants spreads abroad;
looking upward, how is it that it is already midday? For thus it is here at this very moment.
The koyaṣṭika bird perches upon the *kāśmarya* tree whose leaves have emerged,
while the water rushes toward the *aśmantaka* bushes on the bank, its mouth touching the pods.
In the hollow trunk of a *tiniśa* tree, female cranes remain hidden among the water-hens;
below them, the cocks cry out in response to the cooing of the pigeons nesting in the creepers.
Therefore, let it be so; having searched for Mādhava and Makaranda, I shall accomplish what was proposed.
Thus they exit; end of the interlude. Then enter Mādhava and Makaranda.
Makaranda, sighing piteously:
Alas, we are like beasts in that state where the distracted mind neither pursues hope nor abandons it, and enters into the blinding darkness of delusion while accomplishing nothing at all.
Because of the perversity of the Creator, we have fallen into this calamity;
alas, dear Mādhava! O beloved Mālatī, where are you? How is it that this wondrous event remains unknown to me?
O pitiless one, you have been driven to a sudden end; surely, be gracious, show me favor!
O dear Mādhava, why are you so heartless toward me?
Is it not that very hand of mine which, having previously taken the lovely bracelet upon itself, delighted you like a great festival incarnate?
Friend Makaranda, the occurrence of such affection is difficult to find again in this world; yet,
with limbs emaciated by the sap-filled blossoms [of love], there is this great fever of the bodiless god.
Having long endured that which was never-ending in its torment and cruel at every moment,
she resolved to cast away her life as if it were a blade of grass.

What else has been accomplished beyond this, that even the audacity of offering a hand [in marriage] was shown toward me long before the rites of wedding were performed, due to the total disappearance of all hope?

With her cries of weeping— devoid of composure and distressed by the agony of her heart’s core being rent asunder— she manifested such an intent of affection that even I became one whose mind was surging with pain.
[With agitation he said:
"Alas! Indeed, O sir!"
The heart thunders with intense agitation, yet it does not split in two;
the body, though distressed, carries on; delusion does not release consciousness;
and the internal burning inflames the frame, yet does not reduce it to ashes.
Fate strikes the vital organs, yet it does not cut short life.
Makaranda.
Friend, the sun burns mercilessly like a cruel fate,
and such is the condition of your body; therefore, stay for a moment on the bank of this lotus pond.
Please sit here,
for this place is a kinsman to the fragrance thickened by the mingling of the flowing nectar from the beds of young lotuses with upraised stalks.
As you sit after having walked about, the breeze— chilled by the frost of spray from the waves turning before you— will delight you.
Makaranda (to himself):
Let it be so for now; I shall address this openly, my friend Mādhava:
in this [matter], O you with eyes like those of a peacock in rut...
May the divisions of the sky be seen, possessing unceasing splendor, where great lotuses with trembling stalks are shaken, appearing amidst the intervals between the falling and rising of teardrops.
Mādhava rises up with agitation; Makaranda.
How is it that practice is empty? Having risen and proceeded elsewhere, sighing and rising again, O friend, be gracious; look, look!
The dwellings of the forest streams are occupied by thickets of *vānīra* shoots, while at their water's edge, the *yūthikā* flowers are blooming with clusters of buds.
As the clouds spread out like canopies over the mountain ridges where the *kuṭaja* trees bloom and laugh, and where the peaks are embraced by peacocks performing their dances;
and furthermore—

The quarters of the sky, darkened by banks of clouds, become like the grounds of mountain expanses, filled with majestic Kadamba trees that are heavy with the grand display of budding, blossoming, and decaying flowers.
The riverbanks bear lovely *kandala* flowers and blooming *ketaka* blossoms, while the currents of the streams flow on.
O friend, I behold the expanse of forests smiling with the blossoms of the *śilīndhra* and *lodhra* trees now come forth; yet, O Mādhava, they are beautiful while difficult to gaze upon at this time.
The forest lands and mountain regions— why is this so tearful?
Or rather, what else need be said?
The eastern gale blows, carrying the fragrance of blossoming *arjuna* and *sarja* trees.
Rows of glossy clouds resembling fragments of sapphire tumbling from a swinging cradle.
The earth has been sprinkled by showers and has become fragrant; now these days have arrived, carrying the splendor of the transition between the departure of the summer heat and the onset of rain.
Alas, my beloved Mālatī!
There are clouds as dark as young *tamāla* trees, rising thickly and high,
with fresh droplets of water shaken from them by the cool breezes.
How may I now behold the quarters of the sky,
resonant with the sweet, indistinct cries of peacocks and filled with the thundering of Indra’s weapons?
Makaranda gesticulates his affliction with grief:
"The ripening of my friend's current condition is something most cruel."
Sighing with tears, I began once more to offer him diversion, though I was like a thunderbolt.
And thus, O Mādhava, our hope has almost come to an end,
seeing him filled with fear.
How is it that you are utterly bewildered in this void? O Mālatī, Mālatī! What more can be said? Are you devoid of compassion?
O beloved, out of greed for this [wealth], you have committed a rash act here that has cast aside your kinsmen, even though the fault lies with him.
"O friend, who is this that has abandoned the path of compassion? Why does he not yet breathe? Alas, I am robbed by fate!
O Mother, Mother! My heart is bursting; the bonds of my body are falling apart."
I consider the world to be empty; with its unceasing flames, I burn within,
and sinking in blind darkness, my distressed inner self seems to drown.
Delusion shrouds me on all sides; alas, what shall I, of such meager fortune, do?
Oh, what misery! O heart, the festival of moonlight for your kin!
That very moon, charming to Mālatī’s eyes,
this delight of Makaranda and ornament of the world of the living, is now perishing.
Alas, friend Mādhava!
You who were sandalwood paste upon my limbs, the autumnal moon in my sight, and indeed bliss itself within my heart— where are you?
I am destroyed by touching you, who are so intensely desirable, as if Time had suddenly snatched away my very life.
Bestow upon me a gaze radiant with compassion, generosity, and a smile,
and grant me words that are exceedingly harsh.
O dear Makaranda, why do you not acknowledge that your companion, whose heart is devoted to you, has regained consciousness,
Mādhava?
Makaranda (with a sigh of relief):
This [arm] is thick and beautiful with its recently washed royal turban...
By good fortune, the fresh cloud, with its shower of water droplets, has revived my dear friend;
he has, at last, begun to breathe again.
Mādhava:
Therefore, what news of my beloved shall I bring here in this forest to dispel her grief?
Beholding it, he exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
This grove of Jambu trees is dark with the ripening weight of its fruit!"
Breaking apart above the river whose slender waves stumble as it flows northward, a fresh cloud, dark as a mature *tāpiccha* tree, takes refuge on the mountain peak.
Rising up impetuously with his face turned upward and his hands joined in reverence, he said:
"O gentle one, does your dear companion, the lightning, embrace you?"
Either the cātaka birds, their faces bright with manifest affection, resort to it;
or the eastern breeze brings delight with its gentle massages;
or the sky, bearing everywhere the mark of Indra’s bow, spreads its splendor.
Having heard this,
his longing was gladdened as the mountain caves were filled with its echo.
O blue-throated one, with your deep "hum" following your soft, sweet cries, you seem to grant me your consent; therefore,
O divine cloud,
as you wander at will through the world, may you by fate behold my beloved.
Having first comforted her, you should then describe the state of Mādhava;
yet,
while describing it, you must not completely sever the thread of hope.
He alone somehow provides protection for the life of that large-eyed woman;
alas, he has moved away with joy— so I shall go elsewhere.
Makaranda walks about with significance.
How is it now that the eclipse of madness assails the moon of Mādhava? Alas, father!
Alas, mother! Alas, venerable lady, save me, save me! Behold the condition of Mādhava!
Mādhava:
Fie! What a lapse of judgment!
Having crushed [the world], she took her luster from the blossoms of the *lodhra* trees, her gaze from the female deer, her gait from the elephants,
and her gracefulness from the creepers.
It is clear that my beloved has been separated [from me] in the forest— [O] Makaranda,
abode of virtues, dear friend, lord of my life!
Somehow, while her friendship was matured through playing together in the dust,
she now bore the force of the disease of grief born from separation from her beloved.
O heart, though you are shattered, you do not split in two;
indeed, the structural arrangement of Mādhava’s creation is easy for the Creator to imitate in this world.
Let it be so for now;
O sirs, having prostrated myself, I address these beings who roam the mountains and forests.

I make this request: may you favor me by granting your attention for a moment. Has a noble lady, naturally beautiful in every limb, been seen by you while staying here, or has anything regarding her become known to you?
O friends, hear now of her stage of life, wherein the bold Madana operates within her heart, while he remains innocent in her physical form.
Alas, oh alas!
The peacock, with his crest uplifted from the *tāṇḍava* dance, drowns out [the cuckoo's] voice with his cries;
the *cakora* bird, its pupils wandering with intoxication, hastens toward its mate from within its heart's joy.
The golangula monkey dusts his cheek with the pollen of flowers;
whom shall I entreat, for wherever I go, my state as a petitioner is surely swallowed up by an inopportune moment?
And this lovely tooth, reddened by the crimson of her lip, shines forth.
Lifting her face, the bull-lipped one kisses his beloved’s cheek, which is as pale-red as a *kāmpillaka* flower and possesses the luster of a ripe,
crimson, bursting pomegranate.
This elephant, with his trunk resting upon the shoulder of his beloved mate— how can there even be such an untimely moment here?
Scratching with the tip of his tusk his mate, whose eyes were closed in a state of itching,
fanning her with breezes from his ears alternately tossed back and forth,
and gladdening her with half-chewed sprouts of fresh sallakī, he maintained her composure.
While a fortunate wild elephant practices the boldness of familiarity by imagining [the female] elsewhere,
this one, however, looks in another direction.
He does not turn back when the clouds roar with deep thunder,
nor does he take mouthfuls from the nearby lake with its upturned water-moss.

With his face dejected by the loss of his mate, distracted by bees greedy for the ichor of his temples, and surely distressed by the separation from her who is dear as his own life, the elephant is suffering; enough with this torment— he has found his joyful companion once again.
Another leader of a herd of intoxicated elephants, whose sweet and deep throat-roar was being heard, appeared with his temples freshly blossoming.
His temples were smeared with the thick, flowing ichor from his fleshy cheeks, which was saturated with the dense, cool, and fragrant scent of a cluster of *kadamba* flowers; meanwhile,
lotus leaves and petals were scattered about from the fragments of lotus stalks he had torn asunder.
A mass of tender sprouts from filaments, lotus stalks,
and bulbous roots, with a pervasive mist formed by the waves of water shattered by the constant, beautiful, and rhythmic dancing of the *karṇatāla* flapping of [the elephant's] ears.

Having plunged into this lake where the ospreys and cranes are terrified, you sport about; well said, O illustrious lord of serpents! You truly possess praiseworthy youth, and you also have skill in following the will of your beloved; however—
They were made to perform the cutting of mouthfuls of lotus stalks that had been dug up with ease, while being censured.
The transfer of mouthfuls of milk scented with lotuses served as a nourishment;
a sprinkling was performed at will by his spray-emitting hand, yet upon cessation,
out of affection, a parasol of lotus leaves from the stalks between his fingers was held over him.
How can he treat me with such disdain? Alas, I am truly a fool, for I behave toward this forest-dweller as if he were my friend Makaranda. Oh, dear friend!
Fie on this breath of life, which has become a source of slaughter for me thus alone! Fie indeed upon its loveliness, which exists only in the absence of your presence!
May even that day perish which passes here without you; fie upon the mirage of pleasure that arises elsewhere!
Makaranda:
Oh! Even though he is obscured by the delusion of madness, [he perceives] me from some sign.
Or perhaps his innate predisposition toward affection has awakened,
such that he perceives me as standing right before him, even though I am not actually present.
This Makaranda here is indeed your companion; unfortunate Mādhava,
consider me as your dear friend and embrace me, though not my beloved Mālatī.
"O my hope, I am utterly exhausted," says Makaranda, fainting.
Beholding him with compassion, he thought: "I shall honor this lord of my life with joy."
Alas, what misery! Having manifested a longing for my embrace, he has become senseless; therefore, enough now with this calamity of hope.
"It is rightly concluded that I have no friend at all; alas,
my friend,
by whom I was always [regarded] with a heart burning with affection!"
Though I was seized by trembling even without the presence of any cause,
and experienced that entire fear as I contemplated your misfortunes, it has all been pacified for me in an instant.
"Friend, those moments have passed for you which were better, for it was during them that I experienced you as being conscious in such a state; but now— "
The body is a burden, life is a diamond-stake, the quarters of space are empty, the senses are fruitless,
and time is cruel to me now that you have departed.
Having reflected that the world of living beings is everywhere shrouded in darkness, [one should cultivate compassion].
What indeed must I do, being a witness to the setting of Mādhava, that I should continue to live? Let it be; I shall throw myself from this mountain peak into the Pāṭalāvatī river.
I shall become the precursor to Mādhava’s death.
(Walking about a little, turning back piteously, and looking) Alas!
Oh, what misery! What misery!
This very body, possessing the luster of a blue lotus, once belonged to her;
even with my most fervent embraces, I could never find enough of them.
How wonderful! Those glances of Mālatī, which in the past were filled with the playful confusion of fresh love and drank him in with wonder, have now,
in her final years, marveled at such an abundance of virtues in this body.
O friend Mādhava, how did the arrangement of this collection come about?

Therefore, let me embrace my friend even though he has gone such a way; for this very purpose was requested by him, and it must now be fulfilled by embracing him.

Alas, friend Mādhava, treasury of stainless knowledge, teacher of virtues, lord of Mālatī’s life who was won by her own choice, delighter of Kāmandakī and Makaranda, moon-faced one! This final state is yours here in this birth, the very last.
"Friend, the embrace of Makaranda’s arms was what I longed for;
do not think now that Makaranda lives even for a moment.

"It is improper that you alone drink the water of the funeral libation"—
saying this with compassion, she released [the bird], circumambulated it,

May my rebirth occur again and again in that very same place where my beloved friend exists.
